passage: Most adults should aim for roughly 45-65% of daily calories from carbohydrates, 20-35% from fat, and 10-35% from protein, built around vegetables, fruit, whole grains, lean protein and dairy or alternatives.
Added sugars should stay under 10% of daily calories and saturated fat under 10% of daily calories, with most fat coming from unsaturated sources like oils, nuts and fish.
Adults are advised to keep sodium intake under 2,300mg a day, mainly by limiting processed and packaged foods rather than table salt alone.
Adults should get at least 150-300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity, or 75-150 minutes of vigorous activity, per week, spread across most days.
Muscle-strengthening activity that works all major muscle groups is recommended on 2 or more days per week, in addition to aerobic activity.
Some activity is better than none, and benefits start accumulating from the very first minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity, even below the full weekly target.

For workouts longer than about an hour, a carbohydrate-containing snack 30-60 minutes beforehand helps sustain energy, and easily digestible carbs during very long sessions can help maintain performance.
Rather than one large protein-heavy meal, spreading protein across meals and snacks throughout the day supports muscle repair after training.
Drinking water before, during and after exercise helps prevent dehydration; pale yellow urine is a simple everyday indicator of adequate hydration.
A simple way to build a meal is to fill half the plate with vegetables and fruit, a quarter with lean protein, and a quarter with whole grains or starchy vegetables.
Cutting back on highly processed, energy-dense snacks and sugary drinks is one of the most effective ways to reduce excess calorie intake without tracking every gram.
A full meal 3-4 hours before training allows time for digestion, while a smaller carbohydrate-focused snack 30-60 minutes before can top up energy without causing stomach discomfort.

Consuming carbohydrate and protein within about 2 hours after training supports glycogen replenishment and muscle repair; the exact minute-by-minute window is less critical than getting this in during the day.
For sessions over 60-90 minutes or heavy sweating, replacing sodium and other electrolytes alongside fluids helps maintain performance and prevent cramping.
Batch-preparing simple meals built around a protein source, a carbohydrate source and vegetables makes it easier to eat consistently around a training schedule.
Convenient post-training snacks that pair carbs and protein include a yoghurt with fruit, a glass of milk, or a sandwich with lean protein filling.
For people doing regular resistance training, roughly 1.6g of protein per kilogram of bodyweight per day maximises muscle protein synthesis, with little extra benefit found above about 2.2g/kg/day.
Distributing protein into 3-4 meals of roughly 0.4g per kilogram of bodyweight each appears more effective for muscle growth than concentrating it into one or two large meals.

Hitting total daily protein intake is a stronger driver of muscle growth than the exact timing of protein relative to a workout, though eating protein within a few hours of training is still a reasonable habit.
New members are typically advised to start with 2-3 full-body strength sessions a week, focusing on major compound movements, before progressing to more specialised splits.
For general strength and muscle goals, resting 60-90 seconds between sets is a common starting point, with longer rests (2-3 minutes) for heavier, lower-rep lifting.
New members can book a free induction session with a trainer to learn correct form on the main equipment before training independently.
WHO recommends adults do at least 150-300 minutes of moderate-intensity or 75-150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity weekly, plus muscle-strengthening activity on 2+ days.
Limiting long periods of sitting and replacing sedentary time with activity of any intensity is associated with health benefits, independent of meeting the weekly activity target.

Older adults, pregnant and postpartum people, and those with chronic conditions can generally follow the same broad activity targets, adapted in intensity, with balance-focused activity recommended for older adults.
Muscle-strengthening activities include lifting weights, working with resistance bands, bodyweight exercises like push-ups and squats, and heavy gardening or carrying loads.
Stretching and balance exercises, such as yoga or tai chi, are encouraged alongside strength and aerobic work, particularly for older adults to help reduce fall risk.
Allowing at least one rest or light-activity day between intense strength sessions targeting the same muscle groups helps the body recover and adapt.
